alinti: How do we make environments like this for our game, despite both being terrible at 3D modeling?
The secret is a technique called projection.
Our artist starts by drawing every asset on an isometric grid that matches the camera angle in our game.
We then project those drawings onto simple 3D meshes.
Once everything's laid out in the level, we add a few extra layers to bring the environment to life.
We add decals to break up the walls and floors and stop the environment from feeling too repetitive.
For light sources, we use hand-drawn animated flipbooks to keep them consistent with the illustrated style.
Then we use lighting and post-processing to create depth and really sell the illusion that everything's 3D.
This process lets us build stylized environments surprisingly quickly, even though we're only a team of two and neither of us knows how to properly model anything.

alinti: Stop losing your important medical paperwork in a messy drawer.
We've all dealt with that frustration of hunting for an old prescription or a blood test result right when we really need it.
This app, called Cura, acts like a digital filing cabinet for your health records that lives right on your phone.
You just snap a photo of any bill, lab report, or doctor's note, and the app reads the information, organizes everything by date, and even flags if your results are high or low.
It's basically like having a personal assistant who remembers every single doctor visit for you, so you can stop guessing about your history or digging through stacks of paper.
The best part is that it's completely private, because it does all the work directly on your device, without sending your sensitive data to some random server.
If you want, it can even help answer questions about your records, but that's totally optional.
It's a clever way to keep your health details clear and searchable without giving up your privacy.

alinti: Bir ödeme sistemi geliştirdiniz. Kullanıcı bu ödeme sistemini kullanarak 1000 lira ödedi. Ancak kullanıcının kartından o 1000 lira iki kez çekildi.

Örneğin kullanıcı bir ödeme isteği gönderdi. Sunucu isteği aldı. Ödemeyi başarıyla gerçekleştirdi. Ve cevabı kullanıcıya göndermeye çalıştı. Ancak tam o sırada daha da bir problem yaşandı. Ve uygulama bu cevabı alamadı.
Uygulamanın gördüğü şey şu: Ödeme isteğini gönderdim ancak cevap gelmedi. Kullanıcı burada işlemin başarısız olduğunu düşünüp aynı isteği tekrar gönderebilir.
İlk istek aslında sunucu tarafında başarılı tamamlanmıştı. Eğer sunucu gelen ikinci isteği tamamen yeni bir ödeme olarak değerlendirirse kullanıcıdan aynı tutar bir kez daha çekilebilir.
İdempotency'nin amacı aynı isteğin birden fazla kez gelmesi durumunda aynı işlemin tekrar gelmesi ve tekrar tekrar uygulanmasını engellemekte.
Bunun için örneğin her ödeme isteği ile birlikte benzersiz bir Idempotency key gönderilebilir.
Sunucu bu anahtarı kontrol eder. Eğer bu anahtarı ilk kez görüyorsa ödemeyi gerçekleştirir ve oluşan sonucu bu anahtarla ilişkilendirerek kaydeder.
Ancak aynı Idempotency key ile ikinci bir istek gelirse ödemeyi tekrar yapmak yerine daha önce kaydettiği sonucu döndürür.
Kısacası aynı istek tekrarlandığında sistemde yeni bir etki oluşturmuyorsa o işlem idempotent davranıyordur diyebiliriz.

Ever wonder how software companies actually find their security holes?
Most businesses only pay for a professional hacker to test their security once a year, so they're basically leaving the front door unlocked for the other 364 days.
That's where this tool, called Shannon, steps in to change the game.
It's an automated AI that acts just like a security guard for your computer code, constantly checking for weaknesses before your work even hits the public.
Think of it like a smart home security system that doesn't just watch the door, but actively tries to pick the locks to see if they're actually secure.
It looks through the internal structure of your website or app, finds any potential entry points, and runs actual tests to prove if someone could break in.
You get to sleep better knowing that the software you're building has been poked and prodded by an AI that doesn't take breaks.
It's a clever way to stay one step ahead of anyone looking to cause trouble.
Check out the project on the KeyGraph HQ Shannon GitHub page.

If the agent tries to peek at a folder you didn't approve or send data to a website you don't trust, OpenShell just stops it in its tracks.
It even checks its own work to make sure your security rules aren't missing any hidden loopholes before they start.
It's basically a locked room for your agents. It uses AI to do its work without being able to reach anything you want kept private.

alinti: How do Chinese AI companies copy Anthropic models? Anthropic just released a full report explaining how. It says Alibaba collected over 151 million exchanges with Claude in three months to train their Quen models.
The technique is called distillation. You take a stronger model, called the teacher, collect its answers, check their quality, and use them to train your own model, called the student.
Training changes the model's weights, the billions of numbers the model calculates with. First, the model cuts your text into tokens, small pieces of words, and turns each one into a list of numbers.
Then, layer after layer, it multiplies those numbers by its weights. Along the way, it looks back at the earlier words, so it understands each word in context.
During training, the teacher's answer tells the student which token should come next. If the student gives it a low probability, training calculates how to adjust its weights to fix that mistake.
Repeat that millions of times, and the student starts answering like the teacher, without ever contacting it.
But here's the catch. All the numbers in between, called hidden states, stay inside Claude. And Claude only shows the token it picked, not its full probabilities.
So the student only learns from the final text, not from how the teacher got there.
That's why Alibaba went after Claude's thinking, the step-by-step reasoning it writes before answering.
It's the closest thing to seeing how it thinks.
A smaller student also can't hold every skill, and it can learn the examples too closely, then struggle with problems it has never seen. That's called overfitting.
So collecting answers can transfer useful skills. The test is whether your model can solve problems it hasn't seen.

alinti: This GitHub repo just hit number one trending in the world because it fixes the most expensive and unproductive habit in all of AI, vibe coding.
Vibe coding is a complete waste of your time.
Instead, you should be using the skills in this repo to do something called agentic engineering.
Vibe coding is just prompting and hoping for the best.
Super quick to get started, but before you know it, you're stuck, things are breaking, you're going in circles, and you have no idea how you got there or what to do to fix it.
Agentic engineering, on the other hand, is a more structured process where you remain in control at every step of the process.
You're using AI to plan your work, break it down into smaller chunks, and then you're using agents to test what you've created at each step of the process.
This repo lets you start doing that in five simple steps with a set of skills.
Number one is grill meat. Agents will interview you relentlessly until your plan for what you want to build is absolutely crystal clear.
Number two is specs. The agent turns your conversation into a written spec that outlines exactly what's going to be built in plain English.
Number three is tickets. AI breaks that spec down into smaller chunks with technical instructions that AI can then go and implement.
Number four is build. Each ticket is implemented by a new agent with a fresh context window.
And the fifth and last step is a review. The code is checked. Does it pass all your tests? And does it actually match what you had in the spec at the beginning?

And from there, you remain in control. If you need to iterate, don't go in and blindly change the code. All you need to do is change the spec that's written in plain English and then the agent will change the code for you.

alinti: Plexo is a free download manager that uses all your internet connections at once. It's a free, open-source alternative to paid download managers like IDM.

alinti: There's a new cloud technique that's been blowing people's minds this week, and it comes straight from the team that built Cloud. It's called a verification loop, and it fixes the most annoying part of using Cloud. You know when you ask Cloud to build something, and it says it's finished, then you try it, and it's actually broken? Basically, a verification loop makes Cloud test its own work before it ever tells you it's done. So instead of babysitting it, Cloud tries out what it built itself.
So if you ask for a new button on your website, it clicks that button itself and actually takes a screenshot to prove it worked.
When something's broken, Cloud fixes it, tests it again, and keeps going until everything actually works.
The first time, Cloud figures out how to test your project and saves those steps so it runs the exact same test every time after.

alinti: You can now get Opus Clip without paying for it with this one open-source Github repo. It's called Supo Clip and it takes one long video and cuts it into ready post shorts for you so you don't edit everything by hand.
But it doesn't just edit randomly, it actually asks four questions about every single clip.
For example, does the opening hook you? Will people keep watching? Is it actually useful? And would somebody send it to a friend?
So out of a one hour long video, you only get back the clips most likely to go viral.
But the best part is that since it's open source, you run it completely yourself instead of paying every month for the link and setup comment clips.

And you're probably using the wrong one right now.
LOW: brainstorming, a first sketch, renaming a variable. Anything you’ll read line by line anyway.
MEDIUM: a feature you can describe in one sentence. It’s the default on Opus 5.5, and Anthropic says it matches the old Opus on high.
HIGH: a bug in code that already exists. That’s where the edge cases hide.
EXTRA HIGH: the long stuff, like a refactor or a migration.
MAX: when you’re walking away. ‘Find every security hole in this repo, I’ll be back in an hour.’
Type /effort, pick a level, press S.
And it only lasts this session.
Effort isn’t how smart Claude is. It’s how long Claude is allowed to think before it touches your code.
Save this for the next time you open Claude Code.

alinti: This might be the most powerful GitHub repo you can give Claude, and Microsoft open-sourced it.
It gives Claude a sleep cycle. Overnight, it practices the tasks you keep repeating and drafts better instructions, keeping only the changes that test better.
I tell my Claude the same rules every morning. It's like we've never met.
This repo writes it down for you.
It's called SkillOpt from Microsoft Research, and it has over 18,000 stars on GitHub.
Here's one night. It reads your past Claude code sessions, finds the tasks you keep repeating, and practices them again while you're away.
Then it drafts small rule edits for Claude's memory and skills.
Before it keeps an edit, it tests it on tasks it held back on purpose.
Score goes up, the edit is kept. No better, it's thrown out.
And nothing goes live until you type adopt with a backup of the old file.
Okay, how do I get it?

Three steps. One, clone the repo from GitHub. Two, in Claude code, add the plugin from the repo's plugins folder and install SkillOptSleep. Three, type slash SkillOptSleep dry run to preview what it would learn.
Then run, then adopt what you like.
Microsoft's own test with Claude Haiku took a deliberately weak skill from zero to perfect in one night.
The default mode is a free practice run with no AI calls, so switch the back end to Claude for real learning, which uses your own Claude usage.
And real mode sends snippets of your sessions to the model, so skip it on sensitive projects.
The three steps are on DripTheCup.com.
Send this to someone whose Claude keeps forgetting the rules.
